library(flexdashboard)

source("compmus.R")
compmus2025 <- read_csv("compmus2025.csv")

# ---- Shared visual style ------------------------------------------------
ink   <- "#222222"   # text
mine_col <- "#e0a100"   # my tracks (dark yellow)
ref_col  <- "#2b2b2b"   # most danceable track (charcoal)
grey_col <- "#cfcabb"   # all other tracks

# Shared sequential palette for heatmaps, chromagrams, SSMs etc.
# (cream -> mustard -> brown; low values light, high values dark)
dance_cols <- c("#fff6d5", "#f2c230", "#c47a00", "#5a3200")
mine  <- c("wednesday-w-1", "wednesday-w-2")

theme_dance <- function(base_size = 13) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", colour = ink, size = rel(1.1),
                                      margin = margin(b = 4)),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = "#555555", margin = margin(b = 10)),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      axis.title       = element_text(colour = "#333333"),
      axis.text        = element_text(colour = "#555555"),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(colour = "#ebebeb"),
      legend.position  = "top",
      legend.justification = "left",
      legend.title     = element_blank(),
      plot.background  = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      plot.margin      = margin(12, 16, 10, 10)
    )
}

# For chromagrams, cepstrograms, self-similarity matrices, etc.
theme_raster <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_dance(base_size) +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "right")
}

# Corpus scatter plot with a fitted line, my tracks highlighted in yellow
scatter_fit <- function(x, x_lab, title) {
  ggplot(compmus2025, aes(x = {{ x }}, y = danceability)) +
    geom_point(colour = grey_col, size = 2) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = TRUE,
                colour = "#8a6a00", fill = "#f2c230", alpha = 0.25, linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(data = \(d) filter(d, filename %in% mine), colour = mine_col, size = 3.4) +
    labs(title = title,
         subtitle = "Yellow: my two tracks\nLine: linear fit with 95% CI",
         x = x_lab, y = "Danceability") +
    theme_dance()
}

get_conf_mat <- function(fit) {
  outcome <- .get_tune_outcome_names(fit)
  fit |> 
    collect_predictions() |> 
    conf_mat(truth = outcome, estimate = .pred_class)
}  

get_pr <- function(fit) {
  fit |> 
    conf_mat_resampled() |> 
    group_by(Prediction) |> mutate(precision = Freq / sum(Freq)) |> 
    group_by(Truth) |> mutate(recall = Freq / sum(Freq)) |> 
    ungroup() |> filter(Prediction == Truth) |> 
    select(class = Prediction, precision, recall)
}  
cluster_juice <-
  recipe(
    filename ~
      arousal +
      danceability +
      instrumentalness +
      tempo +
      valence,
    data = compmus2025
  ) |>
  step_center(all_predictors()) |>
  step_scale(all_predictors()) |> 
  # step_range(all_predictors()) |> 
  prep(compmus2025) |>
  juice() |>
  column_to_rownames("filename")
compmus_dist <- dist(cluster_juice, method = "euclidean")

# Introduction

Column {data-width=380}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### About this project {.text-card}

#### Research question

What makes a piece of music danceable, and could a calm or melancholic track be turned into a danceable one by changing specific features?

#### Data

The tracks come from AIVA's Styles Library, a collection of tracks generated by an AI model trained in music composition. My two tracks (wednesday-w-1 and wednesday-w-2) are compared against the class corpus of 108 tracks on features such as danceability, arousal, valence, tempo and instrumentalness.

#### Why these tracks

I was particularly drawn to their groove, rhythmic patterns and danceable energy, which made them a good starting point for asking what drives danceability.

#### Approach

1. **Corpus level:** compare the most and least danceable tracks, test simple hypotheses (tempo, arousal, approachability), and train a random forest to tell AI-generated from non-AI tracks.
2. **Track level:** look at mid-level structure in my own tracks (chromagrams, cepstrograms, self-similarity matrices, chordograms, tempograms).

Column {data-width=620}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### Top 5 vs bottom 5 tracks by danceability (standardised features) {.heatmap-card}

```{r}
top5 <- cluster_juice |> arrange(desc(danceability)) |> head(5)
bottom5 <- cluster_juice |> arrange(danceability) |> head(5)

top_plot <- heatmaply(top5,
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          colors = colorRampPalette(dance_cols)(256),
          fontsize_row = 10, fontsize_col = 10)

bottom_plot <- heatmaply(bottom5,
          dist_method = "euclidean",
          hclust_method = "average",
          colors = colorRampPalette(dance_cols)(256),
          fontsize_row = 10, fontsize_col = 10)

subplot(top_plot, bottom_plot, titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE, margin = 0.06) |>
  layout(
    # Labels sit just above each half of the figure, left-aligned,
    # so they never overlap on small screens or get cut off on large ones
    annotations = list(
      list(text = "<b>Top 5</b>  most danceable", x = 0, y = 1,
           xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
           yshift = 6, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 13)),
      list(text = "<b>Bottom 5</b>  least danceable", x = 0.53, y = 1,
           xref = "paper", yref = "paper", xanchor = "left", yanchor = "bottom",
           yshift = 6, showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 13))
    ),
    margin = list(t = 36)
  ) |>
  config(displayModeBar = FALSE)
```

> Using a heatmap, I compared the top 5 most danceable tracks and the bottom 5 least danceable ones to identify distinguishing features.
Surprisingly, I found that higher danceability was more associated with high arousal and valence, but not necessarily with higher tempo.
In contrast, the least danceable tracks tended to have very high instrumentalness and tempo, but scored low on emotional expressiveness (low valence and arousal).
This challenges the common assumption that faster music is always more danceable. Instead, emotional intensity and presence of vocals might matter more.
Because this finding was counter-intuitive, I wanted to further explore why some tracks feel more danceable even if they’re slower, so I shifted from corpus-level to track-level analysis.

# Corpus-Level Analysis

## Column {.tabset}

### Hypothesis 1: Tempo → Danceability

```{r}
tempo_df <- compmus2025 |>
  mutate(
    group = case_when(
      filename %in% mine        ~ "My tracks",
      filename == "roemer-i-2"  ~ "Most danceable track",
      TRUE                      ~ "Other tracks"
    ),
    group = factor(group, levels = c("Other tracks", "Most danceable track", "My tracks")),
    label = if_else(group == "Other tracks", NA_character_, filename)
  ) |>
  arrange(group)   # draw highlighted points on top

ggplot(tempo_df, aes(x = tempo, y = danceability, colour = group)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = group)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.15, vjust = 0.4, size = 3.5,
            fontface = "bold", na.rm = TRUE, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Other tracks" = grey_col,
                                 "Most danceable track" = ref_col,
                                 "My tracks" = mine_col)) +
  scale_size_manual(values = c(2, 3.4, 3.4), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(50, 200), breaks = seq(50, 200, 25)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Tempo vs danceability",
    subtitle = "Black: most danceable track\nYellow: my two tracks",
    x = "Tempo (BPM)",
    y = "Danceability"
  ) +
  theme_dance() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")   # points are labelled directly
```

> **Thinking:**<br><br> Compared to the full dataset, my selected tracks (wednesday-w-1 and wednesday-w-2) exhibit above-average danceability, indicating a strong groove and rhythmic presence.
However, they are not the most danceable—that distinction belongs to roemer-i-2, which sits at the top of the chart.
Interestingly, although my tracks have a higher tempo, they are still outperformed in danceability. This suggests that tempo alone does not determine how danceable a track feels. There might be other influential features at play, such as engagingness, valence, or instrumental texture.

### Hypothesis 2: Arousal → Danceability

```{r}
scatter_fit(arousal, "Arousal", "Arousal vs danceability")
```

> **Thinking:** <br><br> While tempo and approachability showed little or no relationship to danceability, arousal appears to have a weak-to-moderate positive correlation with it.
The plot shows a general upward trend, indicating that more energetic or intense tracks tend to be slightly more danceable.
However, the correlation is not particularly strong—many low-arousal tracks still have high danceability, and vice versa.
This suggests that while energy might help, it is not the sole or strongest factor in determining how danceable a track is.

### Hypothesis 3: Approachability → Danceability

```{r}
scatter_fit(approachability, "Approachability", "Approachability vs danceability")
```

> **Thinking:** <br><br> Although it might seem intuitive that more approachable tracks are also more danceable, this plot reveals no clear linear relationship between the two features.
Songs with similar approachability scores exhibit a wide range of danceability values, suggesting that danceability is not primarily driven by affective features like approachability.
Taken together with the previous hypotheses involving tempo and arousal, this finding leads to a broader conclusion:
Track-level descriptors alone may not sufficiently explain why a piece of music feels danceable.
Instead, as discussed in music structure analysis (Chapter 4), danceability may emerge from deeper mid-level features, such as:
Chroma-based features, which capture harmonic and melodic repetition,
MFCC-based features, which reflect timbral contrast,
and tempograms, which encode rhythmic energy over time.
In short, danceability is not simply a sum of isolated attributes, but a result of how musical elements interact temporally and structurally — across sections, grooves, and repetitions.
Therefore, I decided to shift my focus from the entire corpus to a deeper structural analysis of my own selected track.
By visualizing features such as chromagrams and MFCCs over time, I aim to uncover whether my track contains structural signatures that contribute to its danceability.

### Classification: AI vs non-AI

```{r}
# Random forest: can the five features tell AI-generated from non-AI tracks?
ai_df <- compmus2025 |>
  filter(!is.na(ai)) |>
  mutate(ai = factor(if_else(ai, "AI", "Non-AI")))
ai_formula <- ai ~ arousal + danceability + instrumentalness + tempo + valence

# 5-fold cross-validation, repeated 20 times with different random splits
cv_accuracy <- function(seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  folds <- rsample::vfold_cv(ai_df, v = 5)
  preds <- map_dfr(folds$splits, \(split) {
    train <- rsample::analysis(split)
    test  <- rsample::assessment(split)
    fit <- ranger::ranger(ai_formula, data = train, num.trees = 500,
                          probability = TRUE, seed = seed)
    prob <- predict(fit, test)$predictions
    tibble(truth = test$ai, pred = colnames(prob)[max.col(prob)])
  })
  mean(preds$truth == preds$pred)
}
acc      <- map_dbl(1:20, cv_accuracy)
baseline <- max(table(ai_df$ai)) / nrow(ai_df)

# Feature importance (impurity), averaged over 20 fits on all labelled tracks
rf_importance <- map_dfr(1:20, \(seed) {
  fit <- ranger::ranger(ai_formula, data = ai_df, num.trees = 500,
                        probability = TRUE, importance = "impurity", seed = seed)
  enframe(ranger::importance(fit), name = "feature", value = "importance")
}) |>
  group_by(feature) |>
  summarise(importance = mean(importance)) |>
  mutate(feature = fct_reorder(feature, importance))

ggplot(rf_importance, aes(x = importance, y = feature)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = feature == "tempo"), width = 0.65) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#c47a00", `TRUE` = "#f2d27a"), guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "AI vs non-AI: what matters?",
    subtitle = paste0("Random forest feature importance\nCV accuracy ",
                      round(100 * mean(acc)), "% vs ", round(100 * baseline), "% baseline"),
    x = "Importance (impurity)", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_dance() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12, colour = ink))
```

> **Thinking:** <br><br> To see whether these features also carry information about how a track was made, I trained a random forest (500 trees) to tell AI-generated tracks (n = `r sum(ai_df$ai == "AI")`) from non-AI tracks (n = `r sum(ai_df$ai == "Non-AI")`).
Across 20 repetitions of 5-fold cross-validation it reached an average accuracy of **`r round(100 * mean(acc))`%** (range `r round(100 * min(acc))`–`r round(100 * max(acc))`%), compared with a `r round(100 * baseline)`% baseline from always predicting the larger class.
The features therefore carry some, but limited, information about whether a track is AI-generated.
The model relies most on instrumentalness and arousal, while **tempo is again the least informative feature**, consistent with the danceability results.

# Track-Level Analysis

Column{.tabset}
--------

### Track 1: Chromagram

```{r}
"features/wednesday-w-1.json" |>
  compmus_chroma(norm = "identity") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = pc, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 0:11,
    minor_breaks = NULL,
    labels = c(
                "C", "C#|Db", "D", "D#|Eb",
                "E", "F", "F#|Gb", "G",
                "G#|Ab", "A", "A#|Bb", "B"
              )
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dance_cols) +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_raster()
```

> This track exhibits clear harmonic repetition, with strong vertical striping indicating repeated pitch patterns.
This kind of structure is closely related to groove and may contribute to its danceability.

### Cepstrogram

```{r}
"features/wednesday-w-1.json" |>
  compmus_mfccs(norm = "identity") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = mfcc, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 0:12,
    minor_breaks = NULL,
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dance_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Coefficient Number", fill = NULL) +
  theme_raster()
```

> Track 1 shows stable timbral energy concentrated in lower MFCC coefficients, suggesting a consistent and smooth sonic texture that supports groove.

### Chroma-based

```{r}
"features/wednesday-w-1.json" |>
  compmus_chroma(norm = "identity") |>
  compmus_self_similarity(
    feature = pc,
    distance = "euclidean"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = xtime, y = ytime, fill = d)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dance_cols, guide = "none") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_raster()
```

> Track 1 reveals a highly regular harmonic structure, as shown by the dense and symmetrical grid-like patterns in its chroma-based self-similarity matrix. This indicates strong harmonic repetition—such as loops or consistent chord progressions—which may support the feeling of groove and enhance danceability.

### Timbre-based

```{r}
"features/wednesday-w-1.json" |>
  compmus_mfccs(norm = "identity") |>
  compmus_self_similarity(
    feature = mfcc,
    distance = "euclidean"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = xtime, y = ytime, fill = d)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dance_cols, guide = "none") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme_raster()
```

> Track 1 shows clear sectional structure in its timbre-based self-similarity matrix, with large, cohesive blocks indicating repeated segments. These repeating timbral sections likely reflect a structured form (e.g., A–B–A–C), enhancing rhythmic predictability and supporting groove and danceability.

### Chordogram

```{r}
"features/wednesday-w-1.json" |>
  compmus_chroma(norm = "identity") |>
  compmus_match_pitch_templates(
    key_templates,
    norm = "identity",
    distance = "cosine"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = name, fill = d)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dance_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Template", fill = NULL) +
  theme_raster()
```

> In Track 1, we observe a highly dense and noisy chordogram, with no clear dominant chords over time. This suggests that the harmonic structure is either highly chromatic, constantly shifting, or contains frequent modulations. Such harmonic richness may contribute to expressiveness but may not strongly support predictability or groove — key components of danceability.

### Tempogram

```{r}
"features/wednesday-w-1.json" |>
  compmus_tempogram(window_size = 8, hop_size = 1, cyclic = TRUE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = bpm, fill = power)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dance_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Tempo (BPM)") +
  theme_raster()
```

> The tempogram comparison reveals a clear difference in rhythmic consistency between the two tracks. Track 1 exhibits a stable tempo across its duration, with two dominant bands around 95 BPM and 140 BPM. This suggests a layered, polyrhythmic feel that enhances its groove and danceability.

### Cepstrogram

```{r}

  compmus_mfccs(norm = "identity") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = mfcc, fill = value)) +
  geom_raster() +

> In contrast, Track 2 exhibits more activity in the mid-level MFCCs (especially coefficients 4–6), indicating greater timbral variation across time.
While this variation may add sonic interest and subtle rhythmic motion, it could also disrupt the regularity needed for a strong danceable groove.
Overall, the more homogeneous timbre of Track 1 might contribute to stronger perceived danceability, whereas Track 2's textural complexity could either enhance or interfere with it depending on how listeners interpret the changes.

```

> Track 2, on the other hand, presents a more fragmented and intricate similarity pattern. The lack of strongly defined repeating sections suggests continuous timbral variation, which may offer richness and expressiveness but potentially disrupts the consistency needed for strong perceived danceability.

### Chordogram

```{r}
"features/wednesday-w-2.json" |>
  compmus_chroma(norm = "identity") |>
  compmus_match_pitch_templates(
    key_templates,
    norm = "identity",
    distance = "cosine"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = name, fill = d)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dance_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Template", fill = NULL) +
  theme_raster()
```

> By contrast, Track 2 shows much more structured harmonic repetition. We can see vertical bands, especially around the 25s and 75s marks, where certain chords (like C:maj or F:min) dominate across time. This regularity aligns with the self-similarity patterns previously observed and suggests a more repetitive, section-based harmonic plan. This structure may facilitate listener entrainment and thus support danceability.

### Tempogram

```{r}
"features/wednesday-w-2.json" |>
  compmus_tempogram(window_size = 8, hop_size = 1, cyclic = TRUE) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = bpm, fill = power)) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = dance_cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Time (s)", y = "Tempo (BPM)") +
  theme_raster()
```

> Track 2 shows a more singular dominant tempo around 130 BPM, but it undergoes a noticeable disruption near the 75-second mark. This break in rhythmic flow might interfere with its groove and reduce the sense of momentum, potentially contributing to its lower danceability score.

# Conclusion {data-orientation=rows}

Row {data-height=640}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### Finding 1: Tempo is not the main driver {.text-card}

<div class="stat">
<span class="stat-number">63 BPM</span>
<span class="stat-label">tempo of the most danceable track (roemer-i-2)</span>
</div>

<div class="stat">
<span class="stat-number">100 of 108</span>
<span class="stat-label">tracks in the corpus are faster than it</span>
</div>

**Tempo alone does not determine danceability.** The five most danceable tracks are on average *slower* than the corpus mean, while the five least danceable are *faster*.

### Finding 2: Emotional features matter more

```{r}
group_means <- bind_rows(
  `Top 5`    = top5    |> summarise(across(everything(), mean)),
  `Bottom 5` = bottom5 |> summarise(across(everything(), mean)),
  .id = "group"
) |>
  select(group, arousal, valence, instrumentalness, tempo) |>
  pivot_longer(-group, names_to = "feature", values_to = "z") |>
  mutate(feature = factor(feature, levels = rev(c("arousal", "valence", "instrumentalness", "tempo"))),
         group = factor(group, levels = c("Top 5", "Bottom 5")))

ggplot(group_means, aes(x = z, y = feature)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#b9b2a0", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(aes(group = feature), colour = "#e6dcc0", linewidth = 2.2) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = group), size = 4.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Top 5" = "#5a3200", "Bottom 5" = "#f2c230")) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1.2, 1.2), breaks = c(-1, 0, 1),
                     labels = c("below\naverage", "corpus\naverage", "above\naverage")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_dance() +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12, colour = ink))
```

> Average standardised feature values of the five most and five least danceable tracks. The most danceable tracks score **higher on arousal and valence** and **lower on instrumentalness** (more vocal presence), and they are slower, not faster.

### Finding 3: Structure matters {.text-card}

My two tracks, compared on the track-level plots:

<table class="compare">
<thead><tr><th></th><th>Track 1</th><th>Track 2</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Danceability</td><td><b>0.85</b></td><td><b>0.72</b></td></tr>
<tr><td>Harmony (chroma SSM)</td><td>Regular, grid-like repetition</td><td>More varied, diffuse</td></tr>
<tr><td>Timbre (MFCC SSM)</td><td>Large repeated blocks</td><td>Fragmented</td></tr>
<tr><td>Tempo (tempogram)</td><td>Stable bands at ~95 and ~140 BPM</td><td>~130 BPM, break near 75 s</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

The more danceable track shows **clearer repetition** and **steadier rhythm**, structure that summary features alone do not capture.

Row {data-height=150}
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

### Limitations {.text-card}

The track-level analysis covers only two tracks, so the structural findings are illustrative rather than general. The corpus consists of AI-generated music, so the patterns may not carry over to music in general.
